NEUROANATOMY__Ventricles & CSF:
The big picture: CSF is a clear fluid produced by the choroid plexus inside 4 ventricles (2 lateral, 3rd, 4th). It flows ventricles → subarachnoid space and is reabsorbed into venous blood at the arachnoid granulations. Total volume ≈ 150 mL, but ≈ 500 mL/day is produced — so the whole pool is turned over ~3–4× a day. Block the flow anywhere and pressure rises → hydrocephalus / raised ICP.
The Ventricular System

Four continuous, CSF-filled cavities lined by ependyma. Each connects to the next through a narrow channel — the exam-favourite "chokepoints".

VentricleLocationDrains to → via
Lateral (×2)One in each cerebral hemisphere (body + frontal, temporal & occipital horns + the atrium/trigone, where the choroid plexus glomus lies)3rd ventricle → interventricular foramen (of Monro)
ThirdMidline slit between the two thalami (diencephalon)4th ventricle → cerebral aqueduct (of Sylvius) in the midbrain
FourthBetween pons & medulla (front) and cerebellum (back) — diamond-shapedSubarachnoid space → foramina of Luschka (×2 lateral) + Magendie (median); also continues as the central canal of the spinal cord
Chokepoint = where things block. The cerebral aqueduct is the narrowest part of the whole system → the classic site of obstruction (aqueduct stenosis → non-communicating hydrocephalus). A colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro can suddenly block one/both lateral ventricles.
CSF Circulation — Follow the Flow
💧
Choroid plexus
Produces CSF — mostly in the two lateral ventricles (modified ependymal cells)
↓
🕳️
Interventricular foramen (Monro)
Lateral ventricles → 3rd ventricle
↓
🧠
3rd ventricle → Cerebral aqueduct (Sylvius)
Through the midbrain — narrowest point of the system
↓
🔷
4th ventricle
Exits via foramina of Luschka (×2 lateral) & Magendie (median)
↓
🌊
Subarachnoid space
Bathes the whole brain & spinal cord; pools in cisterns
↓
♻️
Arachnoid granulations → dural venous sinuses
One-way, pressure-dependent reabsorption into venous blood (esp. superior sagittal sinus)
Mnemonic — "Money Sees Large Mansions": Monro → 3rd → Sylvius → 4th → Luschka & Magendie → subarachnoid space.
Production, Functions & Composition
🎯 Functions
  • Buoyancy — the 1400 g brain "weighs" only ~50 g suspended in CSF, protecting it from its own weight
  • Cushioning — shock absorber against trauma
  • Homeostasis — stable ionic environment for neurons
  • Waste clearance — removes metabolites (glymphatic system)
🧪 CSF vs plasma
  • Clear & colourless
  • Glucose ≈ ⅔ of plasma (2.5–4.4 mmol/L)
  • Low protein (0.15–0.45 g/L)
  • Few cells (0–5 lymphocytes/µL; no neutrophils or RBCs normally)
  • Opening pressure 7–18 cmH₂O (adult, lying)
Applied / Clinical Anatomy

Hydrocephalus — too much CSF in the ventricles → they dilate & pressure rises

🚧 Non-communicating (obstructive)
  • Block within the ventricular system
  • Causes: aqueduct stenosis, posterior fossa tumour, colloid cyst (foramen of Monro)
  • Only the ventricles proximal to the block dilate
🌐 Communicating
  • Flow leaves the ventricles but reabsorption fails at the arachnoid granulations
  • Causes: post-meningitis, post-subarachnoid haemorrhage (scarring); rarely overproduction (choroid plexus papilloma)
  • All ventricles dilate
Normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) — a communicating hydrocephalus of the elderly with a normal opening pressure. Classic triad "wet, wobbly, wacky": urinary incontinence + gait apraxia (magnetic/shuffling) + dementia. Potentially reversible with a VP shunt — don't miss it.
Raised intracranial pressure & the LP rule. Blocked CSF flow → raised ICP → headache (worse on lying/coughing), vomiting, papilloedema, falling GCS, and eventually brain herniation (coning). Cushing's triad = hypertension (wide pulse pressure) + bradycardia + irregular breathing = a pre-terminal sign. ⚠️ Never do a lumbar puncture if there is a mass lesion / raised ICP — releasing pressure below can precipitate fatal tonsillar herniation. Get a CT head first.
Lumbar puncture landmarks. The spinal cord ends (conus medullaris) at ~L1/L2 in adults, so an LP is done below it at L3/L4 or L4/L5 — the needle passes through the cauda equina (nerve roots float aside). The intercristal (Tuffier's) line between the iliac crests marks ~L4. Drains: EVD (external ventricular drain, emergency) and VP shunt (ventriculoperitoneal, long-term).
NEUROANATOMY__Applied / Clinical Anatomy:
Neuroanatomy earns its keep at the bedside — lesion localisation. A deficit maps to a place: an artery (stroke territory), a tract (cord syndrome), a nucleus (brainstem syndrome) or a lobe (cortical sign). This subtab pulls the clinically vital patterns together: stroke & brainstem syndromes, cortical localisation, spinal cord syndromes, herniation & raised ICP, intracranial haemorrhage & movement disorders — the “where is the lesion?” toolkit.
Stroke & Arterial Territories
ArteryTerritoryClassic deficit
Middle cerebral (MCA)Lateral hemisphereContralateral face & arm > leg weakness/sensory loss; aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant); gaze deviation towards the lesion
Anterior cerebral (ACA)Medial hemisphereContralateral leg > arm weakness/sensory loss; abulia
Posterior cerebral (PCA)Occipital lobe / thalamusContralateral homonymous hemianopia (with macular sparing)
Lacunar (deep perforators)Internal capsule, pons, thalamusPure motor (posterior limb internal capsule), pure sensory (thalamus), ataxic hemiparesis — no cortical signs
Homunculus rule: the leg is on the medial surface (ACA), the face/hand on the lateral surface (MCA) — so an MCA stroke spares the leg and an ACA stroke hits it.
Brainstem Stroke Syndromes

Rule of crossed signs: a brainstem lesion gives an ipsilateral cranial-nerve deficit with contralateral long-tract (limb) signs — that combination localises to the brainstem.

SyndromeSite / vesselFeatures

Cortical Localisation
Language (dominant, usually left)
  • Broca’s (inferior frontal) → non-fluent, effortful speech; comprehension intact (“Broca = broken speech”)
  • Wernicke’s (superior temporal) → fluent but meaningless speech; comprehension impaired
  • Arcuate fasciculus → conduction aphasia (poor repetition)
Lobe syndromes
  • Frontal — personality change, disinhibition, primitive reflexes, expressive aphasia
  • Parietal (non-dominant) — contralateral neglect; (dominant) → Gerstmann’s (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, L/R disorientation)
  • Temporal — memory, Wernicke’s, superior quadrantanopia (“pie in the sky”)
  • Occipital — homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia
UMN vs LMN facial weakness: an UMN (cortical/stroke) lesion spares the forehead (bilateral cortical input to the upper face); a LMN (Bell’s/CN VII) lesion paralyses the whole half of the face.
Spinal Cord Syndromes
SyndromeTracts affectedSigns

Anterior cordAnterior ⅔ (ASA)Bilateral motor & pain/temperature loss; dorsal columns spared (proprioception preserved)

Herniation Syndromes & Raised ICP
Uncal (transtentorial) → stretches CN III → a fixed, dilated (“blown”) pupil & “down-and-out” eye, then contralateral hemiparesis (or ipsilateral via Kernohan’s notch).
Tonsillar → cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum → brainstem compression & death (never LP a mass with raised ICP).
Subfalcine (cingulate) → under the falx → may compress the ACA.
Cushing’s triad of raised ICP: hypertension, bradycardia & irregular respiration; also headache, vomiting & papilloedema.

Movement, Cerebellar & Pupillary Signs
Basal ganglia & cerebellum
  • Parkinsonism (substantia nigra) — resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia
  • Huntington’s (caudate) — chorea; hemiballismus — contralateral subthalamic nucleus
  • Cerebellar signs (DANISH) — Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning speech, Hypotonia; signs are ipsilateral
Pupils & Horner’s
  • CN III palsy — down-and-out eye, ptosis, dilated pupil (surgical/compressive) vs pupil-sparing (ischaemic/diabetic)
  • Horner’s syndrome — miosis, partial ptosis, anhidrosis (± enophthalmos) from a lesion of the sympathetic pathway (e.g. Pancoast tumour, lateral medullary syndrome, carotid dissection)
  • Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) — optic nerve lesion (Marcus Gunn)
⭐ Exam Pearls
MCA = face/arm > leg + aphasia/neglect; ACA = leg > arm; PCA = homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing).
Lacunar strokes give pure motor/sensory syndromes with NO cortical signs (internal capsule/thalamus/pons).
Brainstem = ipsilateral CN signs + contralateral limb signs (crossed). Wallenberg = PICA/lateral medullary; Weber = midbrain CN III.
Broca = non-fluent (comprehension intact); Wernicke = fluent but nonsense (comprehension lost).
UMN facial palsy spares the forehead; LMN (Bell's) affects the whole half-face.
Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral motor/dorsal column, contralateral pain/temperature. Anterior cord spares the dorsal columns.
Uncal herniation → CN III → fixed dilated pupil; never LP a mass with raised ICP (tonsillar herniation).
Extradural = MMA, lucid interval, lens-shaped; subdural = bridging veins, crescent; SAH = berry aneurysm, thunderclap.
Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral (DANISH); hemiballismus = contralateral subthalamic nucleus; Horner's = miosis/ptosis/anhidrosis.
NEUROANATOMY__Cerebral Cortex & Function:
The cortex is a functional map. Four lobes, split by the central sulcus & lateral fissure, carry discrete Brodmann areas — motor (4), somatosensory (3,1,2), visual (17), auditory (41,42) and the language areas. Each body part occupies a fixed slice of the homunculus. Learn the lobes/landmarks, the primary areas & their Brodmann numbers, the homunculus, the white-matter tracts, and hemispheric dominance — that is the framework every cortical lesion hangs on.
Lobes & Surface Landmarks
Key sulci/fissures
  • Central sulcus (of Rolando) — separates frontal from parietal (motor in front, sensory behind)
  • Lateral fissure (of Sylvius) — separates the temporal lobe below from frontal/parietal above
  • Parieto-occipital sulcus — separates parietal from occipital (on the medial surface)
  • Calcarine sulcus — in the occipital lobe (primary visual cortex)
Lobes (6)
  • Frontal — motor, executive, personality, expressive speech
  • Parietal — somatosensation, spatial awareness
  • Temporal — hearing, memory, receptive speech
  • Occipital — vision
  • Insula (deep to the lateral fissure) — taste, autonomic, interoception; limbic lobe (cingulate/parahippocampal) — emotion & memory
Cortical Histology — the Six Layers
The neocortex (90%) has 6 layers (I–VI, molecular → multiform); the allocortex (hippocampus, olfactory) has 3.
Layer IV (internal granular) receives thalamic sensory input — thick in sensory (“granular”) cortex, absent in motor (“agranular”) cortex.
Layer V (internal pyramidal) is the main output layer — the giant Betz cells of the motor cortex (corticospinal tract) sit here.
Layer VI projects back to the thalamus; layers II/III give cortico-cortical (association & commissural) fibres.

Language loop: Wernicke’s (22) comprehends → the arcuate fasciculus carries it → Broca’s (44/45) produces speech. The angular gyrus (39) & supramarginal gyrus (40) integrate reading/writing.
The Homunculus
Motor (precentral) & sensory (postcentral) cortex are somatotopically mapped as a homunculus — body parts in fixed order.
The leg & foot are on the medial surface (paracentral lobule → ACA); the face, hand & tongue on the lateral surface (→ MCA).
Representation ∝ dexterity/sensitivity — the hand, face & lips are hugely over-represented; the trunk small.
This explains stroke patterns: ACA → leg > arm; MCA → face/arm > leg.
White-Matter Tracts
Three fibre types
  • Association — connect areas within one hemisphere: arcuate/superior longitudinal, uncinate, cingulum, inferior longitudinal
  • Commissural — connect the two hemispheres: corpus callosum (largest), anterior & posterior commissures
  • Projection — connect cortex to subcortex/cord: internal capsule & corona radiata (up & down)
Internal capsule
  • Anterior limb — frontopontine & thalamocortical fibres
  • Genu — corticobulbar fibres (to cranial-nerve motor nuclei)
  • Posterior limb — corticospinal & sensory fibres — a lacunar stroke here → pure motor hemiparesis
Hemispheric Dominance & Lateralisation
The left hemisphere is dominant in ~95% (including most left-handers) → language, calculation, analytical/sequential tasks.
The right (non-dominant) hemisphere → spatial awareness, prosody, face recognition, music; its parietal lesions cause neglect.
The corpus callosum integrates the two; its section (“split brain”) produces disconnection syndromes.
Dominant parietal (angular gyrus) lesion → Gerstmann’s (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia, L/R disorientation).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Central sulcus divides motor (precentral, area 4) from sensory (postcentral, areas 3,1,2).
Betz cells (giant pyramidal) sit in layer V of the primary motor cortex; layer IV (granular) receives thalamic sensory input.
Brodmann: 4 = motor; 3,1,2 = sensory; 17 = vision; 41,42 = hearing; 44/45 = Broca; 22 = Wernicke; 8 = frontal eye field.
Homunculus: leg medial (ACA), face/hand lateral (MCA); hand & face are over-represented.
Wernicke's (comprehend) → arcuate fasciculus → Broca's (produce); damage to the arcuate = conduction aphasia.
Fibres: association (within a hemisphere), commissural (corpus callosum, between hemispheres), projection (internal capsule).
Posterior limb of the internal capsule carries the corticospinal tract → lacunar stroke = pure motor hemiparesis.
Left hemisphere dominant (~95%) for language; right for spatial/prosody; non-dominant parietal lesion → neglect.
NEUROANATOMY__Deep Structures (Basal Gan:
Three deep systems fine-tune movement & relay information. The basal ganglia gate movement through a direct (go) and indirect (stop) pathway balanced by dopamine. The thalamus is the great relay — every sensory modality except smell synapses here before cortex. The cerebellum coordinates movement ipsilaterally. Learn the circuits & their disorders (Parkinson’s, Huntington’s), the thalamic nuclei, and the cerebellar zones, peduncles & signs.
Basal Ganglia — Components
The nuclei
  • Caudate nucleus & putamen = the striatum (the input)
  • Globus pallidus — external (GPe) & internal (GPi) segments (the output is GPi)
  • Subthalamic nucleus (STN)
  • Substantia nigra — pars compacta (SNc, dopaminergic) & pars reticulata (SNr, output)
Groupings (know the names)
  • Striatum = caudate + putamen (input zone)
  • Lentiform (lenticular) nucleus = putamen + globus pallidus
  • Corpus striatum = striatum + globus pallidus (i.e. caudate + lentiform)
  • Output nuclei = GPi + SNr (tonically inhibit the thalamus)
Direct & Indirect Pathways
Direct pathway = “GO”
  • Cortex → striatum (D1) → inhibits GPi/SNr → disinhibits thalamus → thalamus excites cortex
  • Net effect: facilitates (promotes) movement
Indirect pathway = “STOP”
  • Cortex → striatum (D2) → inhibits GPe → disinhibits STN → STN excites GPi/SNr → GPi inhibits thalamus
  • Net effect: inhibits (suppresses) movement
Dopamine (from SNc) excites the direct (D1) and inhibits the indirect (D2) pathway — both actions promote movement. Losing dopamine (Parkinson’s) therefore reduces movement.
Basal Ganglia Disorders
DisorderLesionFeatures
Parkinson’s diseaseLoss of dopaminergic SNc neuronsHypokinetic: resting (“pill-rolling”) tremor, rigidity (cogwheel), bradykinesia, postural instability
Huntington’s diseaseLoss of striatal (caudate) GABA neurons (indirect pathway)Hyperkinetic: chorea, dementia, behaviour change (AD, CAG repeat)
HemiballismusContralateral subthalamic nucleus (often lacunar)Violent, large-amplitude flinging of the limbs
Wilson’s diseaseCopper deposition (putamen)Tremor, dystonia, Kayser–Fleischer rings, liver disease
Hemichorea / tardive dyskinesiaStriatal/dopamine imbalanceInvoluntary choreiform/orofacial movements
Rule of thumb: too little dopamine (or too much indirect) → hypokinetic (Parkinson’s); loss of the indirect brake → hyperkinetic (Huntington’s chorea, hemiballismus).
The Thalamus — the Great Relay

The thalamus relays all sensory modalities except olfaction to the cortex, plus motor & limbic loops. It is divided by the internal medullary lamina (a Y-shaped sheet).

Cerebellum — Anatomy & Functional Zones
Gross & lobes
  • Two hemispheres + midline vermis; three lobes: anterior, posterior & flocculonodular
  • Cortex has three layers: molecular, Purkinje & granular; the Purkinje cell is the ONLY output (inhibitory, GABA)
  • Four deep nuclei (lateral→medial): Dentate, Emboliform, Globose, Fastigial (“Don’t Eat Greasy Food”)
Functional zones
  • Vestibulocerebellum (flocculonodular) → balance & eye movements
  • Spinocerebellum (vermis + paravermis) → posture, gait & trunk
  • Cerebrocerebellum (lateral hemispheres) → planning & coordination of skilled limb movement
Cerebellar Peduncles & Connections
PeduncleDirectionCarries
SuperiorMainly efferent (out)Dentatorubrothalamic fibres → red nucleus & thalamus (→ motor cortex)
MiddleAfferent (in)Pontocerebellar fibres (from the contralateral cortex via pontine nuclei)
InferiorMainly afferent (in)Spinocerebellar & vestibular/olivary input
Ipsilateral rule: cerebellar output double-crosses (dentatorubrothalamic decussation + corticospinal decussation), so a hemisphere lesion causes ipsilateral signs.
Cerebellar Function & Clinical Signs
Signs (DANISH) — Dysdiadochokinesia, Ataxia, Nystagmus, Intention tremor, Scanning (staccato) speech, Hypotonia.
Vermis/midline lesion → truncal ataxia & gait ataxia (fall to no particular side); e.g. alcohol, medulloblastoma.
Hemisphere lesion → ipsilateral limb ataxia, intention tremor, past-pointing, dysdiadochokinesia.
Flocculonodular lesion → nystagmus & balance/vestibular problems.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Striatum = caudate + putamen (input); lentiform = putamen + globus pallidus; output = GPi + SNr.
Direct pathway (D1) promotes movement (disinhibits thalamus); indirect pathway (D2) suppresses it; dopamine favours the direct pathway.
Parkinson's = SNc dopamine loss (hypokinetic); Huntington's = caudate/indirect loss (hyperkinetic chorea); hemiballismus = subthalamic nucleus.
Thalamus relays all sensation except smell: VPL body, VPM face/taste, LGN vision, MGN hearing, VA/VL motor.
Déjerine–Roussy (thalamic) syndrome = contralateral sensory loss + burning central pain (VPL/VPM).
Cerebellar zones: flocculonodular = balance; vermis = trunk/gait; lateral hemispheres = skilled limb movement.
Purkinje cells are the sole cerebellar cortical output (inhibitory/GABA); deep nuclei D-E-G-F lateral→medial.
Cerebellar signs are ipsilateral (double decussation); vermis lesion = truncal/gait ataxia; DANISH.
NEUROANATOMY__Brainstem:
The brainstem is the highway & the switchboard. Three parts — midbrain, pons & medulla — carry every ascending/descending tract, house cranial-nerve nuclei III–XII, and contain the reticular formation (consciousness & cardiorespiratory control). Learn which cranial nerves live at each level, the “motor-medial / sensory-lateral” layout, the key structures on each cross-section, and the vascular syndromes that localise a lesion.
Organisation & the Cranial-Nerve Rule
Three parts & their nerves
  • Midbrain — CN III & IV
  • Pons — CN V, VI, VII & VIII
  • Medulla — CN IX, X, XII (and the cranial/spinal roots of XI)
  • CN I & II are not brainstem nerves (forebrain outgrowths)
Nucleus layout
  • The embryonic sulcus limitans splits nuclei into motor (medial) and sensory (lateral) columns
  • Motor columns (medial→lateral): somatic (GSE — III, IV, VI, XII), branchial (SVE — nucleus ambiguus, motor V, VII), visceral (GVE — Edinger–Westphal, salivatory, dorsal vagal)
  • Sensory columns: visceral (solitary), general somatic (trigeminal), special somatic (vestibular/cochlear)
“Rule of 4”: the somatic motor (GSE) nuclei that divide into 12 are midline — III, IV, VI, XII; the others sit laterally. Motor nuclei of nerves dividing evenly into 12 (3,4,6,12) lie close to the midline.
Cranial-Nerve Nuclei by Level
LevelMotor nucleiSensory / other nuclei
MidbrainOculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), Edinger–Westphal (III parasympathetic)Mesencephalic nucleus of V (proprioception); red nucleus, substantia nigra
PonsMotor V, abducens (VI), facial (VII), superior salivatory (VII)Main (pontine) sensory nucleus of V; vestibular & cochlear (VIII)
MedullaNucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI), hypoglossal (XII), dorsal motor of X, inferior salivatory (IX)Nucleus of the solitary tract (taste & visceral, VII/IX/X); spinal nucleus of V
Trigeminal spans the whole brainstem: the mesencephalic nucleus (midbrain, proprioception), main sensory nucleus (pons, fine touch) and spinal nucleus (pons→upper cord, pain/temperature) — the last explains facial pain loss in the lateral medullary syndrome.
Midbrain
Tectum (roof) = the corpora quadrigemina: superior colliculi (visual reflexes) & inferior colliculi (auditory relay).
The crura cerebri (basis pedunculi — the ventral part of the cerebral peduncles) carry the corticospinal/corticobulbar tracts; the substantia nigra lies just behind them.
The red nucleus & periaqueductal grey (around the cerebral aqueduct) sit in the tegmentum.
CN III emerges from the interpeduncular fossa; CN IV is the only nerve to exit dorsally (and it decussates) — it is also the thinnest/longest intracranial course.
Weber’s syndrome: a lesion of the cerebral peduncle → ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiparesis (crossed sign).
Pons
The basilar (ventral) pons contains the pontine nuclei — relaying cortex → contralateral cerebellum (via the middle cerebellar peduncle) — with the descending corticospinal fibres.
CN V exits mid-pons; CN VI, VII & VIII exit at the pontomedullary junction.
The facial colliculus on the 4th-ventricle floor = the abducens (VI) nucleus with the genu of the facial (VII) nerve looping over it.
The cerebellopontine angle (CN VII & VIII) is the site of a vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma).
Locked-in syndrome: a ventral pontine (basilar artery) infarct → quadriplegia & anarthria with preserved consciousness & vertical gaze.
Medulla Oblongata
The pyramids (anterior) carry the corticospinal tracts, which decussate at the pyramidal (motor) decussation at the cervicomedullary junction.
The olives (inferior olivary nuclei) flank the pyramids; CN XII exits between them (anterolateral sulcus), CN IX/X/XI behind the olive.
The dorsal columns synapse in the nucleus gracilis & cuneatus, whose fibres decussate as the internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus.
The medulla houses the cardiovascular, respiratory & vomiting centres (the area postrema chemoreceptor trigger zone lacks a blood–brain barrier).
Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome (PICA/vertebral): ipsilateral Horner’s, facial pain/temp loss (spinal V), ataxia, dysphagia (IX/X); contralateral body pain/temp loss — no limb weakness. Medial medullary (anterior spinal): ipsilateral tongue (XII) + contralateral hemiparesis.
Reticular Formation
A diffuse network through the brainstem core; the ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) maintains consciousness & the sleep–wake cycle.
Damage to the ARAS (or bilateral thalami) → coma.
Contains the cardiovascular & respiratory centres and modulates pain (descending, via periaqueductal grey → raphe).
Origin of monoaminergic nuclei: raphe (serotonin), locus coeruleus (noradrenaline), and the reticular motor pathways.
⭐ Exam Pearls
Midbrain = CN III, IV; pons = CN V–VIII; medulla = CN IX, X, XII (+XI roots). CN I & II are not brainstem nerves.
Motor nuclei are medial, sensory lateral (sulcus limitans); the GSE nuclei dividing into 12 (III, IV, VI, XII) are midline.
CN IV is the only nerve to exit the brainstem dorsally and it decussates.
Superior colliculus = visual reflexes; inferior colliculus = auditory relay; cerebral peduncles carry corticospinal fibres.
Facial colliculus = abducens nucleus + genu of the facial nerve on the 4th-ventricle floor.
Cerebellopontine angle (VII, VIII) → vestibular schwannoma/acoustic neuroma.
Pyramidal (corticospinal) decussation is in the lower medulla; dorsal-column fibres decussate as internal arcuate fibres.
Weber (midbrain), locked-in (ventral pons), Wallenberg/lateral medullary (PICA), medial medullary — the classic crossed brainstem syndromes.
The ARAS maintains consciousness; its (or bilateral thalamic) damage causes coma.
NEUROANATOMY__Pathways (Sensory, Motor,:
Every pathway is a chain of neurons that crosses somewhere. Know where each tract decussates and you can localise any deficit. Sensory: DCML (fine touch/proprioception — crosses in the medulla) vs spinothalamic (pain/temperature — crosses in the cord). Motor: corticospinal (crosses in the medulla). Plus the visual pathway with its field defects and the auditory pathway. Learn the 3-neuron chains, the crossing points, and the lesion patterns.
Dorsal Column–Medial Lemniscus (DCML)
Modalities & neurons
  • Carries fine (discriminative) touch, vibration, proprioception & two-point discrimination
  • 1st-order — DRG → ascends the ipsilateral dorsal column (gracile = lower limb/below T6; cuneate = upper limb/above T6) → synapse in the nucleus gracilis/cuneatus (medulla)
  • 2nd-order — decussate as the internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus → VPL thalamus
  • 3rd-order — VPL → postcentral gyrus (3,1,2)
Key point
  • Crosses in the medulla — so a cord lesion gives ipsilateral dorsal-column loss below it
  • Damaged in subacute combined degeneration (B₁₂) & tabes dorsalis → sensory ataxia, positive Romberg
Spinothalamic (Anterolateral) Pathway
Modalities & neurons
  • Lateral spinothalamic — pain & temperature; anterior — crude touch & pressure
  • 1st-order — DRG → synapse in the dorsal horn (marginal zone/lamina I & nucleus proprius; the substantia gelatinosa is modulatory)
  • 2nd-order — decussate within 1–2 segments via the anterior white commissure → ascend the contralateral anterolateral cord → VPL thalamus
  • 3rd-order — VPL → postcentral gyrus
Key point
  • Crosses at the cord (near entry) — so a cord hemisection gives contralateral pain/temp loss 1–2 levels below
  • Selectively lost early in a syrinx (central cord → “cape” loss) as crossing fibres are interrupted
The great contrast: DCML crosses in the medulla (so cord lesion = ipsilateral loss); spinothalamic crosses in the cord (so cord lesion = contralateral loss). This is the basis of Brown–Séquard. Face sensation relays via the trigeminal nuclei to VPM.
Corticospinal (Pyramidal) Motor Pathway
Upper motor neuron
  • Primary motor cortex (area 4, Betz cells) → corona radiata → posterior limb of the internal capsule → crus cerebri → pons → medullary pyramids
  • ~85–90% decussate at the pyramidal decussation → lateral corticospinal tract (limbs, contralateral)
  • ~10% stay uncrossed as the anterior corticospinal tract (axial muscles; decussate at their level)
Lower motor neuron
  • The tract synapses on the anterior (ventral) horn cell → LMN → skeletal muscle
  • So the pathway is a two-neuron chain: UMN (cortex → cord) then LMN (cord → muscle)
UMN vs LMN lesion: UMN → spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, up-going plantars (Babinski), no wasting. LMN → flaccid weakness, hyporeflexia, wasting & fasciculations.
Corticobulbar & Extrapyramidal Tracts
Corticobulbar fibres (via the internal-capsule genu) supply cranial-nerve motor nuclei — mostly bilaterally, so an UMN lesion usually spares them.
Exceptions: the lower face (VII) & genioglossus (XII) have mainly contralateral control → an UMN lesion causes contralateral lower-facial droop with forehead sparing.
Extrapyramidal tracts modulate tone/posture: rubrospinal, reticulospinal, vestibulospinal & tectospinal.
Vestibulospinal/reticulospinal drive extensor tone — loss of cortical inhibition underlies decerebrate/decorticate posturing.
Visual Pathway & Field Defects

Retina → optic nerve → optic chiasm (nasal fibres cross) → optic tract → LGN → optic radiation → primary visual cortex (17, calcarine).

Lesion siteField defect
Optic nerveMonocular blindness (that eye)
Optic chiasm (central)Bitemporal hemianopia (e.g. pituitary tumour)
Optic tractContralateral homonymous hemianopia
Meyer’s loop (temporal radiation)Contralateral superior quadrantanopia (“pie in the sky”)
Parietal radiationContralateral inferior quadrantanopia
Occipital (visual) cortexContralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
Rule: defects in front of the chiasm are monocular; at/behind the chiasm they are binocular (homonymous/heteronymous). Meyer’s loop (temporal) carries the upper field → “pie in the sky”.
The Pupillary Light Reflex
Afferent = CN II (optic) → both pretectal nuclei → both Edinger–Westphal nuclei.
Efferent = CN III (parasympathetic) → ciliary ganglion → sphincter pupillae → constriction.
The bilateral pretectal projection is why light in one eye constricts both pupils (direct + consensual).
A relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD/Marcus Gunn) = optic nerve lesion; a CN III palsy = fixed dilated pupil (efferent).
Auditory Pathway
The relay chain
  • Cochlear hair cells → cochlear nerve (VIII) → cochlear nuclei (pontomedullary) → superior olivary nuclei (bilateral) → lateral lemniscus → inferior colliculus → medial geniculate (MGN) → primary auditory cortex (41,42, Heschl’s)
  • Mnemonic: “E.C.O.L.I.M.A.” — Eighth nerve, Cochlear nucleus, Olive, Lateral lemniscus, Inferior colliculus, Medial geniculate, Auditory cortex
Key point
  • Auditory information is bilaterally represented above the cochlear nuclei
  • So a unilateral central (cortical) lesion does NOT cause deafness — unilateral deafness implies a lesion of the ear, cochlear nerve or cochlear nucleus
⭐ Exam Pearls
DCML (fine touch/proprioception/vibration) crosses in the MEDULLA (internal arcuate fibres → medial lemniscus → VPL).
Spinothalamic (pain/temperature) crosses in the CORD within 1–2 segments (anterior white commissure) → VPL.
Cord lesion: dorsal columns ipsilateral, spinothalamic contralateral — the basis of Brown-Séquard.
Corticospinal tract: cortex → posterior limb internal capsule → crus cerebri → pyramids → ~85% decussate → lateral corticospinal tract.
UMN = spastic, hyperreflexia, up-going plantar; LMN = flaccid, hyporeflexia, wasting/fasciculations.
Visual: nasal fibres cross at the chiasm — bitemporal hemianopia = pituitary; homonymous hemianopia = tract/radiation/occipital.
Meyer's loop (temporal) → superior quadrantanopia ("pie in the sky"); occipital lesion spares the macula.
Pupillary reflex: afferent CN II → pretectal → both Edinger-Westphal; efferent CN III → constriction (direct + consensual).
Auditory pathway is bilateral above the cochlear nuclei → a unilateral cortical lesion does not cause deafness.
NEUROANATOMY__Blood Supply:
The brain has two arterial inflows joined by one safety ring. The anterior (internal carotid) and posterior (vertebrobasilar) circulations meet in the circle of Willis, which provides collateral flow. Master the branches of each system, the circle’s components, the arterial territories, the aneurysm sites, and the dural venous sinuses & cavernous sinus — the anatomy behind stroke, SAH and cavernous-sinus thrombosis.
Anterior Circulation — Internal Carotid
Internal carotid branches
  • Ophthalmic artery (→ retina; amaurosis fugax)
  • Posterior communicating artery (to the posterior circulation)
  • Anterior choroidal artery (internal capsule, choroid plexus)
  • Terminal branches: anterior cerebral (ACA) & middle cerebral (MCA)
Deep perforators
  • The MCA gives the lenticulostriate arteries supplying the internal capsule & basal ganglia
  • These are the vessels of lacunar strokes & hypertensive (Charcot–Bouchard) haemorrhage
Posterior Circulation — Vertebrobasilar
The two vertebral arteries (from the subclavians) give the PICA and the anterior/posterior spinal arteries, then unite to form the basilar artery.
The basilar gives the AICA, pontine branches & the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), then bifurcates into the two posterior cerebral arteries (PCA).
Cerebellar arteries: PICA → lateral medulla (Wallenberg); AICA → lateral pons (CN VII & VIII / labyrinthine); SCA → superior cerebellum.
The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (vision) & the inferomedial temporal lobe; it lies near CN III.
The Circle of Willis
An anastomotic ring at the base of the brain linking the anterior & posterior circulations.
Anterior: the two ACAs joined by the single anterior communicating artery (ACom).
Posterior: each PCA joined to the internal carotid by a posterior communicating artery (PCom).
It provides collateral flow if one vessel is occluded — but is often incomplete/variant, and its branch points are the sites of berry aneurysms.
Arterial Territories & Their Strokes
ArteryTerritoryClassic deficit
ACAMedial hemisphereContralateral leg > arm weakness/sensory loss
MCALateral hemisphereContralateral face/arm > leg; aphasia (dominant) / neglect (non-dominant)
PCAOccipital lobeContralateral homonymous hemianopia (macular sparing)
LenticulostriateInternal capsule / basal gangliaPure motor lacunar stroke (no cortical signs)
Watershed zones (between ACA/MCA and MCA/PCA territories) are vulnerable to global hypoperfusion (e.g. severe hypotension/cardiac arrest) → “man-in-a-barrel” proximal-limb weakness & visual disturbance.
Aneurysms & Haemorrhage
Berry (saccular) aneurysms form at circle-of-Willis branch points; the commonest site is the anterior communicating artery.
A posterior communicating aneurysm classically causes a CN III palsy (painful, pupil-involving).
Rupture → subarachnoid haemorrhage (thunderclap headache); risk ↑ with polycystic kidney disease & Ehlers–Danlos.
Hypertensive Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms (lenticulostriates) → deep intracerebral haemorrhage (basal ganglia).
Venous Drainage — Dural Sinuses
The drainage route
  • Superficial cortical veins → superior sagittal sinus; deep veins → great cerebral vein (of Galen) → straight sinus
  • Superior sagittal + straight sinuses meet at the confluence of sinuses → transverse → sigmoid → internal jugular vein
  • Arachnoid granulations (into the superior sagittal sinus) return CSF to the blood
Clinical
  • Bridging veins (cortex → superior sagittal sinus) tear in a subdural haematoma
  • Venous sinus thrombosis → raised ICP, headache, seizures, venous infarct (risk: pregnancy, dehydration, prothrombotic states)
The Cavernous Sinus
Contents (lateral wall, top→bottom): CN III, IV, V₁, V₂; running through the sinus lumen: the internal carotid artery (most medial) & CN VI, which lies free alongside the ICA — the reason CN VI is usually affected first.
Remember: “III, IV, V₁, V₂ in the wall; VI + ICA inside.”
It receives the ophthalmic veins & drains via the inferior petrosal sinus → IJV and the superior petrosal sinus → transverse/sigmoid sinus; it connects to the face via valveless facial veins.
Cavernous sinus thrombosis (from facial/orbital sepsis — the “danger triangle”) → painful ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, chemosis & multiple cranial-nerve palsies (III, IV, VI, V₁/V₂).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Anterior (internal carotid → ACA + MCA) & posterior (vertebrobasilar → PCA) circulations join at the circle of Willis.
Lenticulostriate branches of the MCA supply the internal capsule/basal ganglia → lacunar strokes & hypertensive bleeds.
Cerebellar arteries: PICA (lateral medulla/Wallenberg), AICA (lateral pons, CN VII/VIII), SCA (superior cerebellum).
Circle of Willis: 2 ACAs + anterior communicating; 2 PCAs + posterior communicating to the ICAs.
Commonest berry aneurysm = anterior communicating; PCom aneurysm → CN III palsy; rupture → SAH.
Watershed infarcts (global hypoperfusion) → proximal-limb (man-in-a-barrel) weakness.
Deep veins → great vein of Galen → straight sinus; superficial → superior sagittal sinus; both → confluence → transverse → sigmoid → IJV.
Cavernous sinus: CN III, IV, V1, V2 in the wall; CN VI + ICA inside (VI affected first); thrombosis from facial sepsis.
Arachnoid granulations return CSF to the superior sagittal sinus; bridging-vein tears cause subdural haematoma.
